name: Ouroboros SB-1 'Arbalest'
description:
A vehicle-mounted heavy crossbow platform that fires 1-meter steel bolts weighing 5 kilograms at velocities sufficient to penetrate reinforced concrete walls. The Arbalest uses a hydraulic draw mechanism that charges a bank of torsion springs generating 400 kilograms of draw force, combined with a short electromagnetic acceleration stage that brings the bolt to terminal velocity. The weapon is mounted on a powered gimbal that allows 180-degree traverse and 45-degree elevation from a vehicle roof or fixed position.

Ouroboros developed the Arbalest as a breaching tool for tactical teams that need to penetrate fortified positions without explosive ordnance. A 5-kilogram steel bolt arriving at 200 m/s punches through walls, doors, barricades, and light vehicles with the kinetic energy of a small cannon round, but without the explosive signature, fragmentation hazard, or ammunition regulation of conventional heavy weapons. Like the Longbow, the Arbalest exploits the legal fiction that anything firing a bolt is a crossbow.

The weapon's most common deployment is punching access holes through walls during forced-entry operations — a single Arbalest bolt creates a 15-centimeter breach that operators can use as a firing port, observation point, or anchor for breaching charges. Three bolts in a triangular pattern create a hole large enough for a person to enter. The process is slower than explosive breaching but creates no blast injury risk to occupants the entry team wants alive.
specifications:
bolt length: 1 meter
bolt weight: 5 kg
bolt velocity: 200 m/s
effective range: 150 meters
penetration: 200mm reinforced concrete
reload time: 8 seconds (hydraulic draw)
weapon weight: 85 kg (excluding mount)
mounting: Vehicle roof or fixed emplacement
tactical_use: Structural breaching, fortified position neutralization, and anti-vehicle operations. The Arbalest replaces explosive breaching in operations where blast effects are unacceptable. Vehicle-mounted units provide mobile siege capability for urban operations teams.
cultural_context: The Arbalest is the most absurd example of the crossbow classification loophole — a vehicle-mounted siege weapon that fires 5-kilogram steel spears through concrete walls, legally classified as archery equipment. Its existence has become a running joke in arms regulation discourse and a serious argument for legal reform that will never happen because the manufacturers lobby harder than the reformers.
story_hooks: An Arbalest bolt has been found embedded in the wall of a Tier 5 corporate executive's private residence — fired from street level, it punched through three interior walls before stopping. No follow-up attack occurred. It was a message: we can reach you through your walls.

Someone has mounted an Arbalest on a stolen freight vehicle and is driving through the Gray Zone, firing bolts through the walls of buildings suspected to house corporate surveillance equipment. They're hitting their targets with suspicious accuracy.

physical_description.visual_profile: A brutalist siege weapon resembling a colossal crossbow scaled for vehicular mounting. The Arbalest presents as a compact, purposeful mechanism—all mechanical honesty with no ergonomic softness. Its profile is dominated by a massive torsion spring housing bracketed between twin steel arms, tapering toward a reinforced bolt channel that extends forward like a predator's jaw. The powered gimbal base is a stabilized platform of welded steel and servo-assist hydraulics.
physical_description.dimensions: Overall length: 240 cm (bolt channel), width: 180 cm (spring arm spread), height: 95 cm (above gimbal base). Bolt: 100 cm length. Gimbal mount footprint: 140 × 120 cm.
physical_description.weight_description: Immensely heavy and brutally solid—85 kg of pure mechanical mass designed to absorb 400 kg of spring tension without deflection. When hand-held for inspection, the Arbalest feels like handling structural steel. On vehicle mounts, it settles with the finality of mounted artillery.
physical_description.primary_material: Welded structural steel frame and spring housings. Reinforced aluminum gimbal base. Hardened steel bolt channel and draw mechanism. Composite polymer shock-absorbing pads at pressure points.
physical_description.finish: Industrial matte black powder coat with heavy wear patterns revealing bare steel underneath. Hydraulic components feature brushed steel with minor corrosion from fluids. The bolt channel is polished to a dull sheen from repeated bolt friction. Assembly welds are visible and unfinished—function over aesthetics.
physical_description.color_scheme: Charcoal matte black as primary, with steel gray exposed metal and burnt orange hydraulic fluid staining around connection points. Serpentine Data Centers' logo appears in faded silver.
physical_description.grip_texture: Not user-gripped in traditional sense—the weapon is gimbal-mounted with control via haptic feedback gloves or hardwired targeting systems. Physical access points (adjustment levers, hydraulic pressure valve) are bare knurled steel or rubberized grip tape worn thin from field handling.
distinctive_features: Twin massive coiled torsion spring housings with visible spring arms under extreme tension
Hydraulic pressure gauge mounted on left spring housing, needle often in yellow warning zone
Electromagnetic acceleration coils visible through reinforced polycarbonate window in bolt channel—faint blue capacitor glow when charged
Powered gimbal base with servo motors at traverse and elevation points, marked with worn rotation indices
Heavy bolts stored in reinforced steel magazine cradle—visible 1-meter dark gray shafts with flattened heads
Scorch marks and impact dents from field testing and live-fire breaching operations
Drainage ports and weep holes suggesting aggressive hydraulic fluid management
Hand-painted squad markings and unit designations on gimbal base in silver paint—often obscured by road grime
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Serpentine Data Centers logo (intertwined spiral snake) stamped into left spring housing. Serial plate bolted to gimbal base: 'OUROBOROS SB-1 ARBALEST / SDC-2224-04782'. Hydraulic system placard warning of 400 kg spring tension mounted prominently. Maintenance log plate on base shows field service dates.
physical_description.condition_typical: Well-maintained but obviously deployed. Hydraulic seals show minor weeping, bolt channel has micro-scratches from high-velocity friction, gimbal servos emit faint electronic hum under load. Paint is scuffed from equipment transport and weather exposure. The weapon's condition reflects professional military/paramilitary use—not pristine, but meticulously functional.
